text: You're given the head of a singly linked list, L zero, L one, all the way to L n. Reorder it to L zero, L n, L one, L n minus one, L two, and so on. You may not modify the values in the nodes — only the nodes themselves may be changed.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — I take the first node, then the last, then the second, then the second-to-last, alternating inward. And I have to relink the actual nodes; I can't just shuffle the numbers around. So for one through five I want one, five, two, four, three. And for one through four it'd be one, four, two, three. Are there any constraints on the input size?
Up to fifty thousand nodes. At least one node, so it's never empty.

Let me name the actual difficulty here. Half of what I need is the node from the back — but this is a singly linked list. I can walk forward, and that's it. There's no way to step backward from the tail. So the whole problem reduces to one question: how do I get at the back half without walking the list over and over?

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would be: each time I need the current last node, walk from the head to find it, detach it, and splice it in. That's linear per node for half the nodes, so quadratic — around two and a half billion operations at fifty thousand. Too slow. A second option is to copy the node pointers into a vector and relink from both ends — linear time and correct, since it stores pointers, not values, but it costs linear extra space. This problem reminds me of the reverse-to-walk-backward pattern for singly linked lists. If I reverse the back half, walking backward from the tail becomes walking forward through the reversed half. Then it's three pieces I already know: find the middle with fast and slow pointers, reverse in place, and interleave. Linear time, constant space.

Here's the plan. One: fast and slow pointers from the head, so slow stops where the first half ends. Two: reverse the back half starting at slow's next, then cut. Three: interleave, one node from each half, taking turns. One thing worth flagging is the order in phase two: reverse first, then cut. Slow's next is my only way into the back half, so if I null it out first, the reverse gets a null pointer and the whole back half is lost. And that cut line does two jobs. First, the front half's tail still points at what is now the tail of the reversed half — without the cut, phase three builds a cycle. Second, it also ends the final result; I'll explain why when I get there. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. Three phases plus an iterative reverse helper. Head is already L zero, so I start tail at head and l one at head's next, and each round attaches from the reversed half first, then from the front. That's also why there's no dummy node — I already know the first node, and the function returns void. One thing worth flagging — I never write tail next equals null at the end, and that's deliberate. Phase one leaves the front half longer, by one for odd n and two for even. So the back half runs out first, and the last node I attach is slow, whose next I nulled in phase two. That's the cut's second job.

Let's dry-run the code with one through five, expecting one, five, two, four, three. The rows that matter are phase two. Before the reverse, reaching node five meant walking the list; after it, node five is just the head of the reversed half — one pointer read. In the last round I attach node three and stop. Node three is slow, so its next was already null — the result ends without a termination line. That matches. Corner cases: a single node, where the back half is empty. Two nodes — the back half is empty too, the easiest case to forget. Three nodes, odd, halves differ by one. Four nodes, even, halves differ by two. Since only the length shapes the result, every length from one to two thousand was checked, with a step cap so a cycle can't hang the test.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear — about n over two rounds to find the middle, n over two steps to reverse, and n steps to interleave, so roughly two n pointer operations. Space is constant — a handful of pointers, no allocation. Even at fifty thousand nodes it's linear, and the iterative reverse keeps the stack flat. Oh, one more thing — if I reuse this to check whether a list is a palindrome, the phases carry over but the midpoint rule doesn't. This version leaves the front half longer, which is what lets me skip the termination line. A palindrome check needs balanced halves: with this midpoint, one, zero leaves an empty back half, the comparison never runs, and it wrongly says true. The fix is the loop condition fast next and fast next next. Reuse the structure, re-derive the boundaries.

Strong. Three things stood out. You reduced it to one sentence — singly linked lists can't walk backward, so reverse the part you need to walk backward through — and everything else followed from that. You noticed the cut line does two jobs, and proved the second one from the half-length invariant instead of just asserting the code works. And you skipped the dummy node with a reason, rather than adding one out of habit. Knowing when a pattern doesn't apply is the harder half of knowing the pattern.
